title: Reform, again
tomorrow: who calls God 'master' after escaping real masters?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: old friends. The medieval saints aren't strangers anymore. Today, one of them picks up a pen.
screen: `OLD FRIENDS.` → `ONE OF THEM PICKS UP A PEN.`

segments.voice: The season's over, the locker room is quiet, and someone finally says it: same thing next year? Every team, every family, every church hits that moment. Here's one. A woman from Siena named Catherine, with no office and no title, is sending letter after letter to the pope. He's living in Avignon, in France, far from Rome. She calls him her sweet Christ on earth. Then she tells him, plainly, to come back and be the shepherd he's meant to be. Who writes to a pope like that?
screen: `SAME THING NEXT YEAR?` → `CATHERINE OF SIENA, WRITING.` → `COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Catherine did, and tradition remembers that the pope went back to Rome. Notice what she didn't do. She didn't leave, and she didn't burn it down. She loved the Church enough to call it back to its own shape. That's what reform means here. Paul uses the word in his letter to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "be not conformed to this world; but be reformed in the newness of your mind." Re-formed: given back your form. The Second Vatican Council said something like it about the Church itself. One document calls the Church holy and, at the same time, always in need of being purified. Another speaks of Christ calling the Church to continual reformation while it's still on the road. So two things are true at once: holy, and never finished. Here's the one to tell a friend: Catherine's letters still exist, and she wrote to popes and kings and ordinary people with the same frankness. Reform didn't start with a council for her. It started with one woman who loved the Church too much to stay quiet about it. And the word reaches past the Church. Paul wasn't writing to buildings. He was writing to people, about minds that keep getting made new.
screen: `SHE DIDN'T LEAVE. SHE CALLED IT BACK.` · `BE REFORMED IN THE NEWNESS OF YOUR MIND.` · `HOLY, AND NEVER FINISHED.` · `IT STARTS WITH ONE PERSON.` · then, large: `ALWAYS RENEWING.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing in your life that has slowly lost its shape: a habit, a friendship, a way you pray. Name what it would look like renewed, the one thing in the way, and the smallest first step. If you pray, you can offer that step with Paul's line, be reformed in the newness of your mind.
Reform. To give something back its form: not a new thing, the old thing made new again.
Keep this: always renewing, holy and never finished, the way Catherine loved her Church. See you tomorrow.

You don't have to. Once you're gone, it's honestly their problem to solve.

chat.meaning: Reform means calling something you love back to its shape, from the inside. Catherine didn't leave or tear down; she renewed.

Catherine.meaning: Catherine of Siena, a saint who wrote frank letters to popes

Siena.meaning: a city in Italy, Catherine's home

Avignon.meaning: a city in France where the popes lived for a time

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old English Catholic translation of the Bible

Second Vatican Council.meaning: a gathering of the world's bishops in Rome
